units: a teacher points out to her pupil that the tool warps when the force applied changes
she asks him to go through the movement again slowly
the pupil says he followed the written instructions
the pupil admits he did not grasp the wording of the final point
the teacher explains that heat swells the metal and throws off the reading
she says the source of a fault is seldom where the fault shows
the pupil notices that the cutting waste is winding badly
the pupil works out on his own that the angle of the tool must change
the teacher holds that this reasoning carries over to other machines
she reckons a trade is handed on through an understanding of cause and effect
text: The instructor warns her apprentice that the blade twists the moment his wrist pushes harder or softer. She has him set the tool down and work through the same movement again, slowly. He protests that he followed the written instructions to the letter, then owns up to never having made sense of the wording of the final point. She takes it apart for him: the hand bears down too early, the work heats, the metal swells with the heat, and the reading goes astray. Faults, she adds, seldom begin where they show themselves. The apprentice watches the swarf curling out of the cut and sees that it is winding badly. The angle of the tool has to change, he says, and gets there unaided. She agrees, and tells him that reasoning will carry him through any machine on the floor. A trade, to her mind, passes on as an understanding of what causes what, not as copied movement.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: knowledge once rested on human memory alone
the death of a teacher took part of his doctrine with him
learned circles looked for a lasting remedy
reciting together spread the effort of remembering across several people
a slip by one reciter was caught by another
setting the words down under dictation then held what speech kept badly
the method called for trained copyists and a check made term by term
mistakes of copying became the new danger
checking by two readers comparing aloud put that flaw right
the piling up of these precautions made a doctrine carry across long stretches of time
text: Before writing, all that a community knew rested on memory alone, and that left it badly exposed: when a teacher died, a portion of his doctrine went out with him. Learned circles set about finding a lasting remedy. They took up recitation in company, which spread the burden of remembering across many mouths rather than one. Where a single voice faltered, another carried the line, and the whole survived. Dictation came next, fixing on a surface what speech held badly. It called for trained copyists and a check made term by term. Slips of the pen now became the danger, and the answer to them was a second reading, two people comparing versions aloud, line against line. Piled one on another, these safeguards are why a body of teaching could cross generation after generation without buckling.

units: two ways of teaching a skilled movement exist side by side
the first has the trainer perform while the learner watches and then copies
that route suits flowing movements which words render poorly
it leaves the learner stranded once conditions shift
the second names and justifies every stage
it asks for more effort at the outset
it hands over a rule that holds in other settings
seasoned trainers run the two approaches together
they ask the learner to describe the movement he has just watched
moving between watching and speaking beds the learning down more firmly
text: Two ways of teaching a skilled movement sit side by side, and neither one works everywhere. The first is showing: the trainer performs, the learner watches, then copies. It carries flowing movements across quickly, the very ones that speech handles poorly. Its weakness appears the moment conditions shift, because the learner is left with nothing to steer by. The second is telling: every stage is given a name, an order and a reason. More effort goes in at the start, yet the learner walks away with a rule that holds elsewhere too. Trainers who have been at it a while run the two together. They demonstrate, then insist the learner recount what he has just watched, in his own words. That to and fro between the eye and the tongue beds the learning down far more firmly than either route on its own. The comparison crowns no winner, then. It points to a balance.

units: a neighbour tells of his first days in the workshop of a relative
he builds his account around three memories
he had been given the least steady bench
he grasped that the faulty piece of furniture was part of the test set for him
he laid a pattern the wrong way round and spoiled a stack of boards
the team still find that blunder funny
not one workmate explained anything of his own accord
everything opened up once he began questioning the old hands
the old hands would answer so long as they were asked
he now hands that lesson on to the beginners in his charge
text: A neighbour of mine told me about his first days in his uncle's workshop, and the whole thing came down to three memories. There was the bench: they gave him the wobbliest of them, the one that rocked as soon as any weight went on it, and he worked out soon enough that the furniture was part of the test. There was the stencil: set to mark up a run of boards, he laid the pattern the wrong way round and spoiled the lot, which the team still laugh about. And there was the silence. Nobody explained a thing. A tool went into his hand and that was that. In the end he started asking, and everything opened up. The old hands answered gladly enough. They simply wanted to be asked first. He passes the lesson on now to the beginners under his eye: keep quiet and you learn two years the slower.

units: the session opens with materials being handed out to those taking part
each of them is given a rough piece of wood and a template of stiff card
they check that the corner is true with a measuring tool
any warped piece is set aside at that stage
the outline of the template is carried over in one unbroken line
the trainer sends uneven markings back to be done again
after a break the measurements are carried over onto the other face
that transfer brings every discrepancy out at once
the session ends with everyone showing the mistakes they have put right
cutting is held over until the following meeting
text: In the training workshops where marking out is taught, the session opens with the handing out of materials. Each person is given a rough board and a template cut from stiff card. The square goes against the edge of the board next, so that the corner can be checked as true, and any board that has warped is set aside there and then. Then comes the marking: the outline of the template is followed with a fine point, the hand never lifting mid-line. The trainer walks the benches and sends anyone whose line wavers back to the start. A break follows. Afterwards the measurements are carried over onto the reverse face, which throws up every discrepancy at once. The session closes with everyone gathering round, each holding up the work and naming the mistake put right. No cutting happens before the following meeting.

units: adults are writing again in the room beneath a former storage building
they had left writing behind a very long time ago
a body of local residents lends the premises for nothing
with no official body over it the place spares newcomers the feeling of going back to school
the woman running the sessions says shame turns people away more than the difficulty of the subject
the shape of the room carries the voices
so those taking part hear one another read
that shared listening breeds a rivalry between them
a former factory worker has moved from copying to writing on her own
each stage of her progress leans on the one before it
text: In the low room beneath a former warehouse, a handful of adults are writing again after decades away from it. The building is lent by a cooperative of local residents, and that free loan does what no budget could have bought: since the place answers to no authority, nobody coming through the door feels they are going back to school. The woman who runs the sessions puts it plainly. Shame turns more people away than difficulty ever does. The tables are wide and the ceiling high, so voices carry, and because voices carry, everyone hears everyone else reading. Out of that listening a quiet rivalry grows. A former factory worker describes how she copied first, then dictated to the woman beside her, then wrote on her own. The chain is a patient one, yet each link holds because the one before it held.

units: this training bench can be raised and lowered
its top is pierced with holes at even spacing
beginners hold the work badly and it drifts under the tool
pegs dropped into the holes lock the work without any grip of the hand
the top is of a hard wood that still spares the cutting edges
a rail along the side holds the measuring tools
that stowing keeps the working surface clear
a container underneath gathers the waste from cutting
collecting it that way cuts down the risk of a fall
a groove at the front takes the learner's instruction sheets
text: What strikes you first about a training bench is that it rises and drops to suit whoever stands at it, and that its top is pierced with holes at even spacing. Those holes answer an old problem: a beginner grips the work badly, it creeps under the tool, and the cut wanders off the line. Drop pegs into the holes and the work sits still, with no vice and no strength of hand called for. The top is solid beech, dense enough to take a knock, soft enough to leave a cutting edge alone. A rail along the side holds the square and the rule, which stay within reach instead of cluttering the working surface. Underneath sits a tray that gathers shavings and offcuts, so that nothing ends up underfoot. At the front runs a groove where the learner tucks the instruction sheets. Every part of it answers a difficulty seen in beginners.

units: learning by heart and learning by enquiry are often held to be at odds
the writer finds that rivalry groundless
with nothing held in mind the learner merely gropes about
the learner who does no more than remember recites a contents page without knowing what lies behind it
both of them fail because they pull apart operations that belong together
memorising asks for effort at the outset and then gives effort back
it leaves the attention free for weightier work
enquiry stays costly at every stage
it teaches how to put forward a claim, test it and give it up
the writer urges that the two be combined rather than one of them chosen
text: Learning by heart and learning by enquiry are set against each other far too readily, as though one had to drive the other out. The quarrel strikes me as badly framed. A learner with nothing held in mind does not enquire at all. He gropes about, having no material to put together. A learner who has only committed things to memory recites a contents page without ever having opened the volume. Both fail, and for the same reason: they pull apart what the mind joins. Weigh the effort each of them asks for. Memorising costs at the outset and pays back later, leaving the attention free for weightier work. Enquiry costs at every stage, yet it teaches you to put forward a claim, to test it, and to let it go. One makes for speed, the other for caution. Any serious training measures out both and declines to choose.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: nobody close to her had worked at a craft before she did
her path falls into three parts
she began her apprenticeship while others of her age were still studying
she learned above all by watching an older craftswoman who said very little
she brings damaged books back and rebuilds the parts that have suffered
she turns away any commission that comes with too short a deadline
she first builds a model in plain paper to try out her choices
she keeps her teaching down to two pupils a season by choice
that limit lets her put a movement right as it happens
she will not write a book, holding that the craft passes from hand to hand
text: Nobody in her family had worked with their hands before her. The bookbinder's path falls into three parts. Training first: she took up an apprenticeship at an age when others of her years were still at their studies, and what she learned came mostly from watching the hands of an older woman who said very little. The trade next: she brings damaged volumes back, resews the sections, rebuilds the headbands, and turns away any commission that arrives with a hurried deadline. Before delicate work she builds a dummy of the book in plain paper, so her choices can be tried without the original at stake. Passing it on, last of all: two pupils a season come to her workshop, never more, since she means to catch every movement as it happens. She will not write a manual. One hand, she says, teaches another hand.

units: the writer comes away from this woodworking course in two minds
the opening sessions won him over
a booklet handed out at the start set out a clear progression
the tutor kept to a pace the newcomers could hold
the number taking part swelled because enrolments were accepted too late
those on the course had to wait because there were not enough tools
a good part of each session went by watching other people
the organiser split the group to put matters right
the writer holds that the decision came too late
he would recommend the course only if numbers are capped in advance
text: I came away from this woodworking course in two minds, and it is worth telling in order. The opening sessions really did win me over. We were handed a booklet whose contents page set out a clear progression, and the tutor kept things moving without leaving the newcomers behind. Then the group swelled, because enrolment was left open far too late. From that point on you queued for your turn at the only saw, and half a session could go by watching other people work. The organiser did respond, splitting the group in two, which I was glad enough of, though the remedy arrived very late in the day. The closing sessions clawed back a fair part of the lost ground. I would recommend the course on one condition, that numbers be capped at enrolment. The content is sound. The running of it is not.
